title: Doordarshan
wiki_lead: Doordarshan (lit. 'far sight', i.e. television), abbreviated as DD, is India's state-owned public television broadcaster. Established by the Government of India on 15 September 1959, it is owned by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and constitutes one of Prasar Bharati's two divisions. Doordarshan, one of India's largest broadcasting organisations in studio and transmitter infrastructure, delivers television, radio, online, and mobile services across metropolitan and regional India, and internationally. It also broadcasts via digital terrestrial transmitters.
wiki_excerpt:
Doordarshan (lit. 'far sight', i.e. television), abbreviated as DD, is India's state-owned public television broadcaster. Established by the Government of India on 15 September 1959, it is owned by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and constitutes one of Prasar Bharati's two divisions. Doordarshan, one of India's largest broadcasting organisations in studio and transmitter infrastructure, delivers television, radio, online, and mobile services across metropolitan and regional India, and internationally. It also broadcasts via digital terrestrial transmitters.


History


Beginnings

The channel began modestly as an experimental broadcaster in Delhi on 15 September 1959, with a small transmitter and a makeshift studio. Regular daily transmission commenced in 1965 as part of All India Radio, with a five-minute news bulletin read by Pratima Puri. Salma Sultan joined Doordarshan in 1967 and became a news anchor. Gitanjali Aiyar, Neethi Ravindran, and Rini Simon became popular news anchors in the 1970s.
Krishi Darshan, which debuted on Doordarshan on 26 January 1967, is considered Indian television's longest-running programme.
Television services were expanded to Bombay (now Mumbai) and Amritsar in 1972. By 1975, only seven Indian cities had access to television, with Doordarshan being the sole provider in the country.
On 1 April 1976, television services were officially separated from radio. All India Radio and Doordarshan were placed under the management of separate Directors-General in New Delhi. In 1982, Doordarshan transitioned into a national broadcaster.


Nationwide transmission
National 1 telecasts (DD National) were introduced in 1982. Colour television in India was introduced with the live telecast of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi's Independence Day speech on 15 August 1982, followed by the colour broadcast of the 1982 Asian Games held in Delhi. Two years later, Doordarshan evolved into a structured TV network. The sole TV channel was split into DD-1, a nationally broadcast channel, and DD-2, a city-focused channel. In 1993, they were rebranded as DD National and DD Metro to compete with the then-newly privatised television industry.
According to Mitra, with the start of nationwide transmission in the 1980s Doordarshan began to push a homogenous hegemonic national image of India as a North Indian Hindu Hindi-speaking nation via the broadcast of shows such as Mahabharat (1988 TV series) and Ramayan (1987 TV series). Mitra states Doordarshan's choice of programming depicted other religions, regions, and languages as "marginal or sometimes deviant".
The live telecasts of the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2012 Summer Olympics were aired on Doordarshan's national channel, while DD Sports offered round-the-clock coverage of the event.

grok_lead: Doordarshan is India's autonomous public service television broadcaster, originating as an experimental telecast service launched on 15 September 1959 under the Department of Information Services and All India Radio. It transitioned to regular daily programming in 1965, becoming an independent department within the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting on 1 April 1976, and later integrating into Prasar Bharati upon the latter's formation in 1997 as a statutory body to oversee public broadcasting. Doordarshan maintained a monopoly on television broadcasting in India until the early 1990s, when economic liberalization enabled private channels to enter the market, fundamentally altering the media landscape. During its dominant phase, it prioritized developmental, educational, and cultural content, including initiatives like the 1975 Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE) that delivered programming to rural areas via satellite, fostering national integration and literacy. Iconic serials such as Ramayan (1987â1988) achieved massive viewership, with original broadcasts reportedly reaching tens of millions weekly and pandemic-era reruns drawing claims of up to 77 million viewers for single episodes, underscoring its cultural impact despite debates over exact metrics. As a government-aligned entity, Doordarshan has faced persistent scrutiny for prioritizing state narratives over independent journalism, particularly evident during the 1975â1977 Emergency imposed by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, when it broadcast over 170 of her addresses while systematically excluding opposition viewpoints and enforcing censorship. This episode highlighted the inherent tensions in public broadcasting under authoritarian measures, where empirical control mechanisms suppressed dissenting causal chains of information flow. Today, operating 36 channels and a DTH service from 66 studios, it continues to emphasize public interest programming amid competition, though critiques of political influence persist across administrations.
